newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Assembly seeks to curb pre-trial detention.
newsitem.headline: French Assembly seeks to curb pre-trial detention.

text.p: The French National Assembly approved a draft law on Wednesday aimed at thinning out France's prison population by limiting pre-trial detention.
Almost 40 percent of the men and women held in French prisons are awaiting trial. The duration of such detention is currently open-ended.

The National Assembly voted to limit pre-trial custody to two years for anyone risking a prison term of at least five years. It also adopted an amendment ordering judges to limit pre-trial investigations to one year.

The assembly, dominated by the centre-right, also made it more difficult for judges to detain suspects on fears they would disrupt public order, saying that such a threat had to be exceptional and persistent.

The Socialist opposition voted against the draft bill, which will have to be reconciled with a similar text adopted by the senate before it becomes law, saying it did not go far enough. The assembly's Communist bloc abstained.

"This draft aims to improve our procedures by strengthening the balance which must exist between protection of individual freedoms and the need to combat crime," Justice Minister Jacques Toubon told deputies.
More than 20,000 are in custody awaiting trial. The average period of pre-trial detention in 1995 was four months.

The most notorious person now in pre-trial detention is guerrilla mastermind Carlos the Jackal, who has been in a French jail since August 1994. Before his capture, he had been sentenced in absentia to life in jail for shooting dead two French secret service agents in 1974.
